chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the compurgation (sworn oaths), was a Sunnah established regarding it? He said, 'Yes.' Two men from the Ansar went out to gather fruit, then they separated, and one of the two was found dead. His companion said to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), 'The Jews killed our companion.' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'Make the Jews swear an oath.' They said, 'O Messenger of Allah! How can we make the Jews swear upon our brother, while they are an infidel people?' He (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'So you all swear an oath.' They said, 'How can we swear upon what we do not know and did not witness?' He (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'So the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) paid his blood money from himself.' I said, 'How did the compurgation come to be?' He (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'Indeed, it is the truth, and had it not been for that, people would have killed one another. And indeed, the compurgation is a safeguard by which people are protected.'

key_terms.الْأَنْصَارِ: The Helpers; the residents of Medina who supported the Prophet.
key_terms.الْقَسَامَةِ: Compurgation; a system of sworn oaths used to establish liability in homicide cases.
key_terms.الْيَهُودُ: The Jews; referred to here as a specific community involved in the incident.
key_terms.حَوْطٌ: A safeguard or enclosure; a protective measure.
key_terms.سُنَّةٌ: Sunnah; a established prophetic tradition or practice.

ai.seo_question: What is the origin and legal significance of Qasamah in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi establishes the jurisprudential basis for Qasamah, detailing the Prophet's precedent of accepting the oaths of a specific group (initially the Jews) to determine liability in homicide when eyewitnesses are absent. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) underscores its practical utility as a 'protective enclosure' (hauṭ) for society, preventing unchecked blood feuds by providing a legal mechanism for compensation when direct proof is lacking. This narrative highlights the flexibility of early Islamic jurisprudence in adapting evidentiary standards to communal contexts.
